faq.a: Early ART reduces viral load, preserves immune function, and lowers transmission risk.
faq.q: Why start ART immediately after HIV diagnosis?

faq.a: No definitive cure exists; lifelong ART controls the virus but does not eradicate it.
A paradoxical worsening of a known infection after ART initiation due to recovering immunity.
faq.q: What is immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS)?

exam: What is the WHO clinical stage for a patient with chronic diarrhoea, weight loss >10 % and pulmonary TB? — Stage III; indicates need for ART and TB treatment.

A patient on first‑line ART presents with new cough and fever; sputum GeneXpert is positive for rifampicin‑resistant TB. How do you modify therapy? — Continue ART, start second‑line TB regimen, avoid drug interactions, monitor for IRIS.
Explain why cotrimoxazole prophylaxis is given to all patients with CD4 < 200 cells/µL. — Prevents PCP, toxoplasmosis, and bacterial infections; low cost and high benefit.

A pregnant woman newly diagnosed with HIV at 28 weeks: what regimen should you prescribe and why? — Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir (or efavirenz after first trimester) because of safety and efficacy; avoid nevirapine due to hepatotoxicity risk.

How would you differentiate between HIV‑related lymphadenopathy and lymphoma in a resource‑limited setting? — Look for systemic B symptoms, rapid node growth, and consider fine‑needle aspiration if feasible; lymphoma often has extranodal masses.

What are the key steps if a rapid HIV test is negative but clinical suspicion remains high? — Repeat test after 2‑4 weeks, consider 4th‑generation assay, and counsel on risk reduction while awaiting results.

Describe the management of cryptococcal meningitis in an HIV patient where amphotericin B is unavailable. — Use high‑dose fluconazole induction, monitor renal function, start ART after 4‑6 weeks to reduce IRIS risk.

Why is rifampicin a challenge when starting ART, and how is it addressed? — Rifampicin induces CYP enzymes, lowering levels of many ART drugs; give dolutegravir with an increased dose or delay ART initiation for 2 weeks.
ai.title: HIV Infection and AIDS
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: HIV infection progresses through defined immunologic stages to AIDS, a syndrome of severe immune deficiency. In low‑resource East African settings, co‑infection with TB, hepatitis B and malaria is common and shapes presentation and management.

b: Confirm infection with a 4th‑generation antigen/antibody test or rapid test if lab capacity limited.
Baseline CD4 count and viral load guide staging; if viral load unavailable, use CD4 alone.
sections.p: HIV is a retrovirus that infects CD4+ T‑lymphocytes, leading to progressive immune loss. AIDS is diagnosed when CD4 count falls below 200 cells/µL or an AIDS‑defining illness occurs.

b: Stage I: asymptomatic or persistent generalized lymphadenopathy.
Stage II: minor mucocutaneous manifestations, recurrent upper respiratory infections.
Stage III: weight loss >10 %, chronic diarrhoea, pulmonary TB, severe bacterial infections.
Stage IV: CD4 < 200, or any AIDS‑defining disease (e.g., cryptococcal meningitis, Kaposi sarcoma).
sections.p: The WHO clinical staging system (I–IV) is used where CD4 testing is scarce; it correlates with risk of opportunistic infections.

b: Unprotected sex (most common).
Vertical transmission during pregnancy, labour, or breastfeeding.
Unsafe injections or transfusions.
Occasional occupational exposure.
sections.p: Transmission in East Africa is dominated by heterosexual contact, mother‑to‑child, and contaminated blood products.

b: Acute retroviral syndrome: fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, sore throat (2‑4 weeks post‑exposure).
Chronic phase: weight loss, chronic diarrhoea, oral candidiasis, persistent fever.
AIDS‑defining illnesses: TB, cryptococcal meningitis, Kaposi sarcoma, non‑Hodgkin lymphoma.
sections.p: Early infection may be silent or present with a brief febrile illness. Progressive immune loss produces opportunistic infections and malignancies.
Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Confirms infection; positive result means HIV present, negative requires repeat or alternative assay.
Assesses immune status; <200 cells/µL indicates AIDS, 200‑349 cells/µL suggests high risk of opportunistic infection.
Monitors treatment response; undetectable (<50 copies/mL) indicates effective ART, high (>100 000 copies/mL) suggests failure.
Screens for pulmonary TB or opportunistic pneumonia when sputum microscopy unavailable.
Detects TB and rifampicin resistance; essential in HIV/TB co‑infection.
Looks for anemia, neutropenia, or lymphopenia that may signal opportunistic disease.

b: Acute severe opportunistic infection (e.g., cryptococcal meningitis, severe PCP pneumonia).
TB meningitis or disseminated TB.
Severe diarrhoea with dehydration.
Rapid CD4 decline (<50 cells/µL) or viral load rise despite ART.
sections.p: Identify life‑threatening conditions that require urgent care.

b: First‑line ART (low‑resource WHO regimen): Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir – chosen for potency, high barrier to resistance, and tolerability.
Avoid efavirenz in pregnancy after first trimester; avoid protease inhibitors with rifampicin due to drug‑drug interaction.
Treat TB with standard 6‑month regimen; give rifampicin with ART after 2 weeks of TB therapy to reduce immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS).
Provide cotrimoxazole prophylaxis for CD4 < 200 cells/µL to prevent PCP and bacterial infections.
Screen for hepatitis B and treat with tenofovir‑containing ART if co‑infected.
sections.p: Start lifelong antiretroviral therapy (ART) as soon as diagnosis is confirmed; treat opportunistic infections concurrently.

b: Clinic visit every 3 months: clinical review, adherence counseling, CD4/viral load if available.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B, pneumococcus, and seasonal influenza.
Educate on safe sex, condom use, and partner testing.
Provide mother‑to‑child transmission prophylaxis: maternal ART, infant nevirapine for 6 weeks, and exclusive breastfeeding with maternal viral suppression.
sections.p: Regular monitoring ensures treatment success and early detection of complications.

b: Severe malnutrition – also causes weight loss and low CD4‑like counts but improves with nutrition.
Chronic hepatitis B – can cause lymphopenia but lacks opportunistic infections.
Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome – rare in adults, presents with lymphadenopathy but no viral load.
False‑negative rapid HIV test during acute infection – repeat after 4 weeks if high clinical suspicion.
CD4 count may be artificially low during acute infections; repeat after treating the acute illness.
Chest X‑ray may miss early TB; combine with GeneXpert when possible.
